text: Mirza Hameedullah Beg (M. H. Beg) (22 February 1913 – 19 November 1988[1]) was the 15th Chief Justice of India, serving from January 1977 to February 1978. Born into a Deccani Muslim family, his father Mirza Samiullah Beg was the Chief Justice of Hyderabad State, making him a significant figure in Hyderabad state affairs. He was the real uncle of internationally acclaimed beautician Shahnaz Husain. Like many aristocratic children in Hyderabad at the time, Mirza Hameedullah Beg attended St. George's Grammar School, where he earned a gold medal for securing first position in the Senior Cambridge H.S.L.C. Examination. Under British influence, wealthy Indians commonly pursued higher education in England, particularly in law. Thus, M.H. Beg joined Trinity College and Cambridge University in 1931, earning Honours in Archaeological and Anthropological and Historical Triposes, and studied law, economics, and politics at the London School of Economics. He joined the bar through the Honourable Society of Lincoln's Inn and was called to the Bar in England in 1941. After graduation, he returned to India and began practising as an Advocate at the Allahabad and Meerut High Courts. In 1949, he enrolled as an Advocate of the Federal Court of India and later became an Advocate of the Supreme Court of India. He built an extensive legal practice, serving as Standing Counsel to the U.P. Sunni Central Wakf Board and frequently appearing for Municipal bodies. Beg was raised to the Bench of the Allahabad High Court on 11 June 1963, where he sat on both Criminal and Civil sides as well as on the Tax Bench. From mid-1967 to 1970, he served as Company Judge and oversaw the matrimonial and testamentary jurisdiction of the High Court. Following the reorganization of territories and the establishment of Himachal Pradesh, M.H. Beg was appointed Chief Justice of the Himachal Pradesh High Court in January 1971.[2] After a brief tenure, he was elevated to Judge of the Supreme Court of India on 12 December 1971, during which he authored 194 judgments and sat on 562 benches.[3] As Chief Justice of India, he administered the oath of office to the 6th President of India, Neelam Sanjiva Reddy. He was involved in the landmark Habeas Corpus case, Additional District Magistrate of Jabalpur v. Shiv Kant Shukla, which arose in 1975 during the Indian Emergency. The case centered on whether citizens' right to judicial scrutiny for arrests was suspended during emergency. The five senior-most judges heard the case, with four aligning with the government's view that even the right to life was suspended (only H. R. Khanna dissented). In his April 1976 decision, Justice Beg observed: "We understand that the care and concern bestowed by the state authorities upon the welfare of detenues [sic?] who are well housed, well fed and well treated, is almost maternal."[4] A few months later, in January 1977, M.H. Beg, who was junior to H. R. Khanna, was appointed Chief Justice of India by the Indira Gandhi government—a move that violated legal tradition, despite having started with A. N. Ray's appointment. This interference in judicial independence was widely protested;[5] subsequent law ministers, especially Shanti Bhushan, introduced measures to place judicial appointments under the authority of the Chief Justice rather than the executive. After Mohammad Hidayatullah, Beg was the second Muslim Chief Justice of India. After a one-year term, he retired in February 1978. Subsequently, he served as chairman of the Minorities Commission of India.[6][7] While practising as an Advocate, he held various faculty positions teaching different subjects. Since retirement, he has written two books discussing Muslim politics in India.
